title: Prime Factors, HCF and LCM Flashcards

cards.front: $$42 \div 6$ gives 7 exactly. What does this show about 6?

options.explanation: A factor divides a number exactly with no remainder. Since $42 \div 6 = 7$, the number 6 is therefore a factor of 42.
This reverses the factor-multiple relationship. Since $42 \div 6$ is an integer, 6 is a factor of 42, while 42 is a multiple of 6.
This reverses the direction of divisibility: 42 does not divide 6 exactly. The calculation shows that 6 divides 42 exactly, so 6 is a factor of 42.
The quotient 7 is not automatically a factor of the divisor 6. The exact division $42 \div 6 = 7$ shows that 6 is a factor of 42.

cards.front: Why is 1 not a prime number?

options.explanation: A prime number must have exactly two distinct positive factors: 1 and itself. For the number 1 these are the same factor, so it has only one.
Counting 1 twice as both 1 and itself is a common mistake. Distinct factors are counted only once, so 1 has one factor and is not prime.
The number 1 divides itself exactly, so it does have a positive factor. It is not prime because it has only one distinct factor, rather than exactly two.
Evenness is determined by divisibility by 2, and 1 is odd. Its actual reason for not being prime is that it has only one distinct positive factor.

cards.front: A prime number has exactly [ ___ ] factors: 1 and [ ___ ].
cards.back: A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself.

options.text: A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself.
options.explanation: By definition, a prime number has exactly two distinct positive factors. These are always 1 and the prime number itself.

options.text: A prime number has exactly one factors: 1 and itself.
options.explanation: Treating 1 and the number itself as one factor confuses prime numbers with the number 1. A prime has two distinct factors: 1 and itself.

options.text: A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and 2.
options.explanation: Only the prime number 2 has 2 as its second factor. In general, every prime has exactly two factors: 1 and itself.

options.text: A prime number has exactly three factors: 1 and itself.
options.explanation: Having three factors does not satisfy the definition of a prime number. A prime has exactly two distinct positive factors: 1 and itself.

cards.front: A prime factorisation should never include [ ___ ].
cards.back: A prime factorisation should never include 1.

options.explanation: The number 1 is not prime, so it cannot appear as a prime factor. Including it also adds no useful information because multiplying by 1 changes nothing.
Although 0 should not appear in a prime factorisation, it is not the intended defining exclusion here. Prime factorisations never include 1 because 1 is not a prime number.
The number 2 is the smallest prime and is included whenever it divides the original number. It is 1 that must never appear because 1 is not prime.
The number 3 is a valid prime factor and should be included when it divides the number. A prime factorisation never includes 1 because 1 is not prime.

cards.front: What does $2^3$ mean in index notation?

options.explanation: An exponent tells you how many times the base is used as a factor. Therefore, $2^3$ means multiplying three factors of 2 together.
Multiplying the base by the exponent is a common index error. The exponent 3 means use 2 as a factor three times, giving $2 \times 2 \times 2$.
This incorrectly uses the exponent as the repeated factor. In $2^3$, the base 2 is repeated three times, so it means $2 \times 2 \times 2$.
An index represents repeated multiplication, not repeated addition. Since the base is 2 and the exponent is 3, the expression means $2 \times 2 \times 2$.

cards.front: Write 84 as a product of prime factors.

options.explanation: Dividing 84 gives $84 = 2 \times 42 = 2 \times 2 \times 21 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 7$, and every factor on the right is prime.
One factor of 2 has been omitted, so the right-hand side equals 42 rather than 84. The complete factorisation is $84 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 7$.
The exponent on 3 has been increased incorrectly, making the product three times too large. There is only one factor of 3, so the correct power is $3^1$.
This includes one extra factor of 2, so the product is 168 rather than 84. There are exactly two factors of 2, giving $2^2 \times 3 \times 7$.

cards.front: For HCF using prime factors, which primes do you keep?
cards.back: Primes that appear in every number.

options.text: Primes that appear in every number.
options.explanation: The HCF must divide every number, so only prime factors shared by all the numbers can be included. Any unshared prime would prevent the result dividing at least one number.

options.text: Primes that appear in any number.
options.explanation: Keeping every prime that appears in at least one number is the method associated with finding the LCM. For the HCF, retain only primes appearing in every number.

options.text: Primes that appear in one number.
options.explanation: A prime found in only one number cannot be part of a common factor. For the HCF, keep primes that occur in every number being considered.

options.text: Primes that are below every number.
options.explanation: A prime being smaller than each number does not mean it divides them. The HCF uses only prime factors that appear in every number’s prime factorisation.

cards.front: For HCF, choose the [ ___ ] power of each shared prime.
cards.back: For HCF, choose the smallest power of each shared prime.

options.explanation: A common factor cannot contain a prime more times than any number being compared. Therefore, the HCF uses the smallest exponent of each shared prime.
Choosing the largest power is the rule used for the LCM, not the HCF. The HCF must divide every number, so it uses the smallest shared power.
Adding the powers would introduce too many copies of the prime and produce a result that may not divide every number. The HCF uses the smallest shared power.
Averaging exponents is not part of finding an HCF and could even produce a non-integer exponent. The HCF takes the smallest power of each shared prime.

cards.front: Given $54 = 2 \times 3^3$ and $126 = 2 \times 3^2 \times 7$, find the HCF.

options.explanation: For the HCF, use each common prime at its smallest power: $2^1 \times 3^2 = 2 \times 9 = 18$.
This uses only one factor of $3$ instead of the shared $3^2$. Taking the smallest common powers gives $2 \times 3^2 = 18$.
This omits the factor $2$, even though both numbers contain it. The HCF includes $2^1$ and $3^2$, giving $18$.
This copies the first number, but $3^3$ is not a factor of $126$. The smallest shared powers are $2^1$ and $3^2$, giving $18$.

cards.front: For LCM using prime factors, which primes do you include?

options.explanation: The LCM must be divisible by every original number, so it includes every prime appearing in any factorisation, using the greatest required power of each.
Including only shared primes is the method for finding an HCF. An LCM includes every prime that appears in any of the numbers.

options.text: Every prime in the first number.
options.explanation: Restricting the selection to the first number can omit factors needed for divisibility by the others. The LCM includes every prime that appears.
The numerical size of a prime does not determine whether it is included. The LCM requires every prime appearing in any of the factorisations.

cards.front: For LCM, choose the [ ___ ] power of each prime.
cards.back: For LCM, choose the largest power of each prime.

options.explanation: The LCM must contain enough of each prime to be divisible by every number, so the largest power of each prime is selected.
Choosing the smallest power is the HCF method because it keeps only factors common to every number. For an LCM, choose the largest power.
The first power would include each prime only once, which may not provide enough factors. The LCM uses the largest power shown.
Restricting the choice to a common power confuses LCM with HCF. For the LCM, select the largest power of every prime that appears.

cards.front: Given $45 = 3^2 \times 5$ and $60 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 5$, find the LCM.

options.explanation: The LCM uses the largest powers present: $2^2 \times 3^2 \times 5 = 4 \times 9 \times 5 = 180$.
This is the HCF, found from the shared factors $3 \times 5$. The LCM uses the greatest powers of all primes, giving $180$.
This keeps only $3^1$, so the result is not divisible by $45$, which contains $3^2$. Using $3^2$ gives an LCM of $180$.
This is obtained by multiplying $45$ and $60$ and then dividing incorrectly. Their shared factors must not be duplicated, so the LCM is $180$.

cards.front: Two regular events repeat at fixed intervals. What calculation gives the next time together?
cards.back: Find the LCM of the intervals.

options.text: Find the LCM of the intervals.
options.explanation: Each event occurs at multiples of its interval. The first positive time that is a multiple of both intervals is their lowest common multiple.

options.text: Find the HCF of the intervals.
options.explanation: The HCF measures the greatest interval that divides both values; it does not give their next shared occurrence. That time is found using the LCM.
Adding the intervals does not generally produce a multiple of each one. The next time both events occur together is given by their LCM.
The product is a common multiple but may not be the first one, especially when the intervals share factors. The next meeting uses the LCM.

cards.front: Before using LCM in a time question, put all intervals in [ ___ ].
cards.back: Before using LCM in a time question, put all intervals in the same units.

options.explanation: LCM compares whole-number intervals directly, so all times must first be expressed in one unit, such as converting hours and minutes entirely into minutes.
Applying LCM to mixed units compares unlike quantities and gives an invalid result. Convert every interval into the same units before calculating the LCM.
Choosing the largest unit can introduce fractions and is not the requirement. All intervals must be converted into the same units before finding the LCM.
Small units are often convenient, but they are not always necessary. The essential requirement is that every interval is expressed in the same units.

cards.front: A tram and coach both arrive at 10:00, then every 9 and 12 minutes. When next together?

options.explanation: The LCM of $9$ and $12$ is $36$, so both services return together $36$ minutes after 10:00, which is 10:36.
This adds the two intervals, but $21$ is not a multiple of either $9$ or $12$. Their LCM is $36$, giving 10:36.
This uses only the coach's interval. After $12$ minutes the tram is not due, since $12$ is not a multiple of $9$; both return at 10:36.
This multiplies the intervals to get $108$ minutes, which is a shared return time but not the next one. The LCM is $36$ minutes, giving 10:36.

cards.front: For $P = 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5$ and $Q = 2^2 \times 3 \times 7$, find the HCF.

options.explanation: The common primes are $2$ and $3$. Taking their smallest powers gives $2^2 \times 3^1 = 4 \times 3 = 12$.
This incorrectly reduces the shared power of $2$ from $2^2$ to $2^1$. The smallest powers actually present are $2^2$ and $3^1$, giving $12$.
This uses $3^2$ from $P$, but $Q$ contains only $3^1$, so $36$ cannot divide $Q$. Using the smaller powers gives $12$.
This includes the factor $7$, which appears only in $Q$ and is therefore not common. The shared prime powers produce an HCF of $12$.

cards.front: For $P = 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5$ and $Q = 2^2 \times 3 \times 7$, find the LCM.

options.explanation: The LCM uses the highest power of each prime present: $2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5 \times 7 = 2520$.
Using $2^2$ instead of the higher power $2^3$ misses a factor of $2$. The LCM is $2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5 \times 7 = 2520$.
Multiplying by an unnecessary extra factor of $3$ makes the result three times too large. Using each prime’s highest power gives an LCM of $2520$.
Omitting the factor $5$ gives $504$, but the LCM must contain every prime factor needed by either number. Including $5$ gives $2520$.

cards.front: Given $12 = 2^2 \times 3$, $18 = 2 \times 3^2$, and $30 = 2 \times 3 \times 5$, find the HCF.

options.explanation: The common prime factors with the lowest powers are $2^1$ and $3^1$. Therefore, the HCF is $2 \times 3 = 6$.
This includes the common factor $2$ but overlooks that all three numbers are also divisible by $3$. Their HCF is therefore $2 \times 3 = 6$.
This includes the common factor $3$ but overlooks that all three numbers are also divisible by $2$. Their HCF is therefore $2 \times 3 = 6$.
Taking the highest powers resembles the LCM method and makes the result too large; $12$ does not divide $18$ or $30$. The HCF is $6$.

cards.front: Given $12 = 2^2 \times 3$, $18 = 2 \times 3^2$, and $30 = 2 \times 3 \times 5$, find the LCM.

options.explanation: The LCM uses the highest power of every prime present: $2^2 \times 3^2 \times 5 = 180$, which is divisible by all three numbers.
Using only one factor of $3$ overlooks the $3^2$ in $18$, so $60$ is not divisible by $18$. The correct LCM is $180$.
Using only one factor of $2$ overlooks the $2^2$ in $12$, so $90$ is not divisible by $12$. The correct LCM is $180$.
Including an unnecessary extra factor of $2$ doubles the smallest common multiple. The highest required powers give $2^2 \times 3^2 \times 5 = 180$.

cards.front: Two numbers are coprime if their HCF is [ ___ ].
cards.back: Two numbers are coprime if their HCF is 1.

options.explanation: Coprime numbers share no prime factors, so their only positive common factor is $1$. Consequently, their highest common factor is $1$.
An HCF is a positive factor shared by the numbers, and every whole number has $1$ as a factor. Coprime numbers therefore have HCF $1$, not $0$.
An HCF of $2$ means both numbers are even and share the prime factor $2$, so they are not coprime. Coprime numbers have HCF $1$.
At GCSE, the HCF is defined as the greatest positive common factor, so it cannot be negative. For two coprime numbers, the HCF is $1$.

cards.front: Two numbers have HCF 6 and LCM 72. After taking out the HCF, what do the leftover parts multiply to?

options.explanation: Writing the numbers as $6a$ and $6b$, where $a$ and $b$ are coprime, gives an LCM of $6ab$. Therefore, $ab = 72 \div 6 = 12$.
Multiplying by the HCF counts the common factor again instead of removing it. Dividing the LCM by the HCF gives the leftover product: $72 \div 6 = 12$.
Dividing by $6^2$ removes the common factor twice. The LCM contains one shared factor of $6$, so the leftover parts multiply to $72 \div 6 = 12$.
Taking out a common factor requires division, not subtraction. Dividing the LCM by the HCF gives the product of the coprime leftover parts: $72 \div 6 = 12$.

cards.front: Two whole numbers greater than 8 have HCF 6 and LCM 72. Find them.

options.explanation: The numbers are $6 \times 3$ and $6 \times 4$. Since $3$ and $4$ are coprime and multiply to $12$, the HCF is $6$ and LCM is $72$.
These numbers have HCF $12$ and LCM $36$, so neither required value is obtained. The pair $18$ and $24$ has HCF $6$ and LCM $72$.
Although the LCM is $72$, both numbers are divisible by $12$, making their HCF $12$ rather than $6$. The required numbers are $18$ and $24$.
Although the LCM is $72$, these numbers share a factor of $12$, so their HCF is $12$. The pair with HCF $6$ is $18$ and $24$.
